summary:
We developed SPHEREx Time-Lapse Explorer, an open-source interactive web platform that transforms multi-epoch near-infrared observations (0.75–5.0 μm) from NASA’s SPHEREx space telescope into chronological time-lapses, false-color composites, and astrometrically aligned difference maps.

Directly addressing the "Planet X and SPHEREx" challenge, our tool queries NASA/IPAC IRSA SIAv2 services in real time to retrieve raw FITS cutouts across 102 spectral bands. It aligns multi-epoch images using World Coordinate System (WCS) reprojection, normalizes flux via Z-score statistics, and highlights moving objects—such as brown dwarfs, asteroids, and potential Planet X candidates—as automated trajectory dipoles. Additionally, it cross-matches ESA Gaia DR3 and NASA AllWISE catalogs, propagating proper motions to the exact observation epoch (MJD) alongside aperture photometry light curves and animated GIF exports.

This solution is important because it eliminates the technical barriers of complex FITS data processing, empowering citizen scientists and researchers worldwide to visually discover faint, fast-moving celestial bodies from any web browser.
details:
What Does It Do & How Does It Work?

Every night, NASA’s SPHEREx space telescope quietly scans the cosmos across 102 near-infrared spectral bands (0.75–5.0 μm), capturing millions of faint photons that hold the secrets of our solar system’s outer frontier. Yet for most people, that universe remains locked behind complex, multi-dimensional FITS files and specialized command-line tools.

SPHEREx Time-Lapse Explorer was born from a simple, powerful conviction: the thrill of astronomical discovery should belong to everyone. Our web platform connects in real time to NASA/IPAC IRSA SIAv2 archives to retrieve raw spectral cutouts for any coordinate in the sky—or one-click validation targets like Barnard’s Star, WISE 0855, Epsilon Indi B, RW Aurigae, and R Draconis. Through an automated astrometric pipeline, it sorts observations by Modified Julian Date (MJD), applies astrophysical ZScale normalization, aligns multi-epoch frames using World Coordinate System (WCS) reprojection (reproject_interp), and generates:

• Chronological Multi-Band Time-Lapses & Start-vs-End Blink Comparators to visually spot motion.

• False-Color Infrared RGB Composites using non-linear arcsinh stretching to reveal ultra-cool thermal signatures.

• Astrometric Difference Maps (Final - Initial) with Z-score flux normalization that highlight moving objects as automated cyan-to-gold trajectory dipoles (#1–#5).

• Live Catalog Cross-Matching with ESA Gaia DR3 and NASA AllWISE, propagating proper motions (mas/yr) to the exact observation epoch via SkyCoord.apply_space_motion().

• Central-Aperture Photometry Light Curves and instant animated GIF exports.

Benefits & Intended Impact

By turning raw telemetry into intuitive visual stories, we empower students, educators, amateur astronomers, and citizen scientists anywhere in the world to become active explorers. A faint, uncataloged moving dipole in the outer solar system—whether an asteroid, a rogue brown dwarf, or even Planet X—no longer requires a supercomputer to be noticed; it only requires human curiosity and a web browser.

Tools, Languages and Software Stack

• Backend & Astrophysics Engine: Python 3, FastAPI, Uvicorn, Astropy (FITS, WCS, Time, SkyCoord), Reproject, SciPy, NumPy, Matplotlib, and Pillow.

• Frontend & Visualization: Vanilla HTML5, CSS3, responsive dark-space UI, and deep-link URL state sharing (/?ra=...&dec=...&size=...).

• Open Data Infrastructure: NASA/IPAC IRSA SIAv2 & SCS APIs, ESA Gaia DR3 TAP, and GitHub.

Creativity and Key Factors Considered

True scientific creativity lies in bridging precision with simplicity. While building the tool, we solved critical real-world observational challenges: eliminating telescope roll-angle rotation artifacts between epochs, accounting for multi-year proper motion shifts between catalog epochs (J2010.5/J2016.0) and current SPHEREx captures, and implementing resilient server fallbacks and local caching so exploration never stops. Above all, we designed every pixel around human wonder—because when we open the doors of NASA’s data to the world, anyone can help find what is hiding in the dark.
